Populations of the blind catfish Pimelodella kronei inhabit subterranean river systems where thermal conditions remain remarkably stable. At a water temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C], field observations indicate that reproductive ecology follows a constrained seasonal pattern. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) is approximately 4.5% [GSI = approximately 4.5%] under stable thermal conditions of 19 °C [T = 19 °C]. This value, though derived from a related epigean species, offers a useful comparative benchmark for assessing reproductive investment in the troglobitic P. kronei. The constant temperature regime of 19 °C is a critical backdrop for interpreting this and other physiological measurements, as it dictates metabolic rates and developmental schedules throughout the subterranean life cycle. Furthermore, the age at which the free-swimming larva emerges from the egg at this temperature has been documented, with the onset of the yolk-sac larva stage occurring after an incubation period of approximately 10 days [ab = approximately 10 days] at 19 °C [T = 19 °C].

As the yolk-sac larva undergoes yolk absorption and initiates exogenous feeding, the juvenile fish begins a protracted trajectory toward sexual maturation. The total length at which puberty is attained has been established at 10 cm [Lp = 10 cm], a size that marks the onset of gonadal development and the transition from the immature juvenile phase to the early stages of reproductive viability. At this same developmental milestone, the corresponding wet weight at puberty has been calculated to be 7.8 grams [Wwp = 7.8 grams], based on length-weight relationships derived from morphometric data. This size threshold is of considerable interest for understanding life-history trade-offs in hypogean fishes, where energy acquisition is limited by reduced food availability in the aphotic zone. Reaching sexual maturity at a relatively modest body size compared to epigean congeners may represent an adaptive response to the low-energy environment, allowing individuals to begin reproduction earlier despite slower growth rates. These metrics of length and mass at puberty provide essential baseline data for constructing a life-history profile of this endemic troglobitic species.

The ultimate or asymptotic total length represents the theoretical maximum size an individual can attain and is a key parameter in describing the species' growth trajectory. For Pimelodella kronei, the ultimate total length has been estimated at 20.2 cm [Li = 20.2 cm], a value that suggests a moderate body size relative to other members of the Heptapteridae. Corresponding to this asymptotic length, the ultimate wet weight, calculated from the length-weight allometry specific to this species, reaches 62.7 grams [Wwi = 62.7 grams]. The attainment of this maximal size likely occurs over many years under the slow metabolic regime dictated by the constant temperature of 19 °C. Once an individual reaches this size, somatic growth effectively ceases, and energetic resources are channeled primarily into maintenance and reproductive effort. This ultimate mass, at over eight times the weight recorded at sexual maturity, underscores the substantial somatic growth that occurs during the prolonged adult phase of this long-lived cave fish.

Longevity data for Pimelodella kronei, presumably recorded under the stable thermal conditions of 19 °C [T = 19 °C], indicate a maximum lifespan of 15 years [am = 15 years]. This extended lifespan is notably high for a fish of its relatively small final body size and likely reflects the low metabolic demands and reduced predation pressure characteristic of the subterranean habitat. The absence of large predators in the cave environment may allow individuals to allocate energy toward long-term somatic maintenance and repeated reproductive events over many seasons. This iteroparous life-history strategy, coupled with a protracted juvenile phase, contrasts markedly with the faster-paced life cycles of many epigean siluriforms. The documented longevity, when considered alongside the age at hatching of 10 days [ab = 10 days], highlights the extreme disparity between the brief, energetically dense incubation stage and the extended, low-energy adult lifespan that is a hallmark of troglobitic adaptation at a temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C].

A comparative analysis of life-history metrics reveals the profound influence of the aphotic environment on the biology of Pimelodella kronei. The wet weight at birth, estimated at 0.0012 grams [Wwb = 0.0012 grams] based on an egg diameter of 1.3 millimeters, is exceedingly small and reflects the limited maternal provisioning typical of many teleosts that produce numerous pelagic eggs. The yolky egg incubates at 19 °C [T = 19 °C], and the larva begins its benthic existence at a minimal body mass. The transition from this 0.0012 gram hatchling to the 62.7 gram [Wwi = 62.7 gram] asymptotic adult represents an over fifty-thousand-fold increase in body mass. This dramatic growth trajectory, occurring over a lifespan of 15 years, is sustained by feeding on nutrient-poor allochthonous detritus and small invertebrates carried into the cave system. The combination of a minute initial mass, a late age at sexual maturity marked by a total length of 10 cm, and an exceptionally slow growth rate to a maximum length of 20.2 cm, paints a clear picture of a species adapted to a resource-limited, low-disturbance environment.
